title: Durable Publication on a Crashing Machine
learning_objectives: Distinguish durability from atomicity and say which one fsync provides
State the four-step publication order and why each step precedes the next
Explain why the containing directory must be synchronized after the rename
Choose between the replacing and non-replacing rename for a given destination
Name what each crash window leaves behind and why none of them leaves a mixture

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: A program writes a file, and the machine loses power mid-write. What comes back is neither the old version nor the new one. It is torn, and every later step will trust it anyway.
segments.spoken_text: A program writes a file, and the machine loses power mid-write. What comes back is neither the old version nor the new one. It is torn, and every later step will trust it anyway.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: Start with what a successful write promises. The kernel copies your bytes into the page cache and returns. The device sees them later. A crash in between loses bytes you thought you had written.
segments.spoken_text: Start with what a successful write promises. The kernel copies your bytes into the page cache and returns. The device sees them later. A crash in between loses bytes you thought you had written.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: Order is not promised either. A filesystem may make a later write durable before an earlier one, so a crash can leave a state you never passed through.
segments.spoken_text: Order is not promised either. A filesystem may make a later write durable before an earlier one, so a crash can leave a state you never passed through.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: Two words carry the whole lesson. A byte is durable when it survives a power loss with no further help from the program that wrote it.
segments.spoken_text: Two words carry the whole lesson. A byte is durable when it survives a power loss with no further help from the program that wrote it.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: A change is atomic when every reader sees all of it or none. Durability is about surviving a crash; atomicity is about what a reader can observe.
segments.spoken_text: A change is atomic when every reader sees all of it or none. Durability is about surviving a crash; atomicity is about what a reader can observe.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: So, a question to sit with. If you call fsync and it returns, which of those two properties have you bought?
segments.spoken_text: So, a question to sit with. If you call fsync and it returns, which of those two properties have you bought?

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: Durability, and only durability. The bytes are on the device. A reader can still open that file and find content complete but wrong for its name.
segments.spoken_text: Durability, and only durability. The bytes are on the device. A reader can still open that file and find content complete but wrong for its name.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: Torn content and torn visibility are different failures. fsync answers the first and says nothing about the second: the name is separate from the bytes.
segments.spoken_text: Torn content and torn visibility are different failures. fsync answers the first and says nothing about the second: the name is separate from the bytes.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: The answer to the second is rename. Within a single filesystem, rename swaps one directory entry for another in a single metadata operation.
segments.spoken_text: The answer to the second is rename. Within a single filesystem, rename swaps one directory entry for another in a single metadata operation.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: That is why rename, not the write, is the commit point. A reader resolves the name to the old file or the new one, never to something half written.
segments.spoken_text: That is why rename, not the write, is the commit point. A reader resolves the name to the old file or the new one, never to something half written.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: So publication is four steps in one order. Serialize into a temporary file beside the destination. Synchronize that file. Rename it over the destination. Synchronize the containing directory.
segments.spoken_text: So publication is four steps in one order. Serialize into a temporary file beside the destination. Synchronize that file. Rename it over the destination. Synchronize the containing directory.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: Said as steps: write the staging file; synchronize it; rename it over the destination; synchronize that directory; append the event. The order is the whole thing.
segments.spoken_text: Said as steps: write the staging file; synchronize it; rename it over the destination; synchronize that directory; append the event. The order is the whole thing.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: The file is synchronized first because the rename is what makes it reachable under the real name. Rename first, and the name resolves to content the device may not hold.
segments.spoken_text: The file is synchronized first because the rename is what makes it reachable under the real name. Rename first, and the name resolves to content the device may not hold.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: Here is the mistake almost everyone makes. The rename returned, so the new version is in place and the work is done.
segments.spoken_text: Here is the mistake almost everyone makes. The rename returned, so the new version is in place and the work is done.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: It is not. A rename changes a directory, and a directory is data the kernel can hold in memory. Atomic, yes. Durable, not yet.
segments.spoken_text: It is not. A rename changes a directory, and a directory is data the kernel can hold in memory. Atomic, yes. Durable, not yet.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: What exactly is still at risk after the rename returns and before you synchronize the directory?
segments.spoken_text: What exactly is still at risk after the rename returns and before you synchronize the directory?

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: The directory entry. A crash there leaves the old name in place, with the new file complete on the device but referred to by nothing.
segments.spoken_text: The directory entry. A crash there leaves the old name in place, with the new file complete on the device but referred to by nothing.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: That is why the fourth step exists. Synchronizing the containing directory is what makes the new name itself survive.
segments.spoken_text: That is why the fourth step exists. Synchronizing the containing directory is what makes the new name itself survive.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: You might object that this scatters temporary files everywhere, and that a crash before the rename leaves garbage on disk.
segments.spoken_text: You might object that this scatters temporary files everywhere, and that a crash before the rename leaves garbage on disk.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: To be precise about what it leaves: a staging file no authoritative name refers to. The destination still holds the previous complete version.
segments.spoken_text: To be precise about what it leaves: a staging file no authoritative name refers to. The destination still holds the previous complete version.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: So it is a recoverable outcome, not corruption. Inspect that file or discard it; nothing reading the destination was affected.
segments.spoken_text: So it is a recoverable outcome, not corruption. Inspect that file or discard it; nothing reading the destination was affected.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: It also explains why staging happens in the destination's own directory. A rename cannot cross a filesystem boundary at all: it fails rather than copying, and a copy-and-delete fallback is not atomic.
segments.spoken_text: It also explains why staging happens in the destination's own directory. A rename cannot cross a filesystem boundary at all: it fails rather than copying, and a copy-and-delete fallback is not atomic.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: One more distinction. Rename has a variant that refuses to replace anything: it publishes only if the destination name is still free.
segments.spoken_text: One more distinction. Rename has a variant that refuses to replace anything: it publishes only if the destination name is still free.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: Which one you want depends on what the name means. A cache entry is content addressed, so its name already claims what it holds; publish it once, never replace it.
segments.spoken_text: Which one you want depends on what the name means. A cache entry is content addressed, so its name already claims what it holds; publish it once, never replace it.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: A job document is the opposite. It is authoritative state that legitimately moves forward, so replacing it is correct, each replacement a four-step publication.
segments.spoken_text: A job document is the opposite. It is authoritative state that legitimately moves forward, so replacing it is correct, each replacement a four-step publication.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: Cache entry or job document: which one do you publish with the refusing form of rename, and why?
segments.spoken_text: Cache entry or job document: which one do you publish with the refusing form of rename, and why?

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: The cache entry. Its name is a claim about its bytes, so an overwrite changes what a reader already trusts under that name.
segments.spoken_text: The cache entry. Its name is a claim about its bytes, so an overwrite changes what a reader already trusts under that name.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: One step is left, and it comes last. The event recording the change is appended after the authoritative state is durable, never before.
segments.spoken_text: One step is left, and it comes last. The event recording the change is appended after the authoritative state is durable, never before.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: An event describing a state the system never reached is worse than no event, because recovery reads that log to decide what happened.
segments.spoken_text: An event describing a state the system never reached is worse than no event, because recovery reads that log to decide what happened.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: Walk the crash windows. Before the file is synchronized, the destination is unchanged. Between that and the rename, still unchanged, with a staging file left over.
segments.spoken_text: Walk the crash windows. Before the file is synchronized, the destination is unchanged. Between that and the rename, still unchanged, with a staging file left over.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: Between the rename and the directory synchronization, the old version or the new one, both whole. After it, the new version, durable. No window yields a mixture.
segments.spoken_text: Between the rename and the directory synchronization, the old version or the new one, both whole. After it, the new version, durable. No window yields a mixture.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: That whole discipline rests on one assumption worth saying aloud: rename is atomic within a single filesystem. The destination and its staging file must live on the same one, and the guarantee does not carry to a mount that emulates it.
segments.spoken_text: That whole discipline rests on one assumption worth saying aloud: rename is atomic within a single filesystem. The destination and its staging file must live on the same one, and the guarantee does not carry to a mount that emulates it.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: Compressed to one line: stage beside the destination, synchronize the file, rename, synchronize the directory, then log.
segments.spoken_text: Compressed to one line: stage beside the destination, synchronize the file, rename, synchronize the directory, then log.

segments.speaker: instructor
segments.display_text: What that buys you is this. A machine that dies at an arbitrary instant comes back holding one of exactly two reviewed states. Nothing is left to repair.
segments.spoken_text: What that buys you is this. A machine that dies at an arbitrary instant comes back holding one of exactly two reviewed states. Nothing is left to repair.
